Textbooks

Relevant Software Tools for the Course

  • PLECS
    • Circuit simulator built for power electronics: switching converters, control loops and thermal behaviour, solved and implemented much faster than in LTSpice
    • Setup and licensing: instructions on D2L
  • Typhoon HIL Control Center (for final projects)
    • Real-time hardware-in-the-loop platform: your control code runs on real hardware while the power stage is emulated
    • Debug the controller on its own instead of two coupled systems, and iterate quickly with no equipment at risk. There is no need to install the software as it will already be available on the ENA 13 computers but you must make an account.
    • To obtain V-HIL license, follow the instructions here: Access Free V-HIL License

Please set up PLECS and obtain your V-HIL license as soon as possible.

Planned Topics for this Course

Converters we will study (in order)
  • Non-Isolated DC-DC Converters
  • Isolated DC-DC Converters
  • Single-Phase Inverters
  • Diode and Phase-Controlled Rectifiers
  • Three-Phase and Grid-Connected Converters
  • Resonant Converters and Soft Switching
Through this course, you will learn
  • How the converters operate, and when to use each one
  • How to analyze them, including small-signal modelling
  • How to design converters for new applications
  • How to close the loop: feedback compensator design
  • How to validate a design experimentally against your model

Projects

Take a converter from concept to a working, measured prototype — and explain why it behaves the way it does. 40% of the course grade.

Select parts from lab for selected topology → model and compensator design → simulate → HIL validation → bench bring-up → demo

What you will do

  • Own hardware is possible — talk to me first. Otherwise, use parts from the lab
  • Design review with me, then supervised bench sessions
  • Demo your working converter, plus a short individual Q&A + final report

Power Electronics is a Multidisciplinary Field

Involves:

  • Semiconductor devices
  • Embedded systems
  • Control systems
  • Electrical circuits
  • Batteries
  • EMI/EMC
  • Analog/digital circuits
  • Magnetics
  • Machines
  • Mechanical design
  • Thermodynamics
  • …

What are Power Electronic Circuits?

  • Power electronic circuits convert electrical energy from the form supplied by a source to the form required by the load

Example: Grid supply (120 V AC, 60 Hz) → motherboard (12 V DC).

Converters Change the Character of Electrical Energy

  • From dc to ac
  • From ac to dc
  • From one voltage level to another
  • From one frequency to another

Power electronic circuits are often referred to as converters.

The Topology Manipulates the Flow of Energy

  • E.g. Buck converter, dual active bridge converter

Ex. Flyback Converter

A Real Converter is More Than its Topology

  • But if you look at a reference design you will see that there are many other elements that must be added beyond the circuit elements required for this topology.

The Supporting Circuitry Around the Topology

  • These additional circuit elements may include:

    • Input and output filters
    • Gate driver circuits
    • Sensor circuits
    • Controllers
    • Auxiliary power circuits
    • Protection circuits
    • Thermal management (heat sinks), etc.

Our Focus: the Converter Circuit Itself

  • While these elements are all important, they do not affect the primary function of the circuit.
  • While we will touch on some of these aspects in the course, we are mostly focused on power electronic converter circuits. More specifically:
    • How does this circuit operate?
    • How to analyze this circuit?
    • How to design power electronic converters based on this circuit for new applications?
    • How to control these power electronic converters?

Why can’t we use a resistor divider to convert voltages in a power application?

What is the power delivered by the source, \(P_{source}\)?

\[ I_{source}=I_{load}=\frac{12\,\mathrm{V}}{6\,\Omega}=2\,\mathrm{A} \]

\[ P_{source}=24\,\mathrm{V}\cdot 2\,\mathrm{A}=48\,\mathrm{W} \]

What is the efficiency?

\[ \eta_{eff}=\frac{P_{load}}{P_{source}}\cdot 100\%=50\% \]

Other than the low efficiency, do you all see other issues with this type of approach for stepping down a voltage?

Lossless Property of Ideal Converters

  • With a couple of exceptions, a key feature of a power electronic circuit is that it is ideally lossless*
  • Exception 1: Low Dropout Regulator (LDO)
  • Exception 2: Electronic Load

Working Through an Ideal Converter: 24 V in, 12 V out

  • Let’s take as an example an ideal converter that delivers 2 A to a load. The source voltage is 24 V and the load voltage is 12 V.

What is the power to the load, \(P_{load}\)?

\[ P_{load}=12\,\mathrm{V}\cdot 2\,\mathrm{A}=24\,\mathrm{W} \]

For this ideal converter, what is the power delivered by the source, \(P_{source}\)?

\[ P_{source}=P_{load}=24\,\mathrm{W} \]

For this ideal converter, what is the current from the source, \(I_{source}\)?

\[ I_{source}=\frac{24\,\mathrm{W}}{24\,\mathrm{V}}=1\,\mathrm{A} \]

What direction is the source current flowing?

  • Out of the source (i.e. clockwise)

Building Blocks: Only Lossless Elements Allowed

Therefore, a power converter must be made up of circuit elements that are ideally lossless (i.e. no resistors). What might some of these circuit elements be?

  • Switches*
  • Inductors
  • Capacitors
  • Transformers

In the ideal form, all of these elements are lossless. *In LDOs and electronic loads, the switches are operated in such a way that they by definition are lossy (i.e. MOSFETs operating in the linear region).

Switch-Mode Circuits: Fully On or Fully Off

  • The focus of the course is on switch-mode power electronic circuits (i.e. not LDOs and electronic loads)
  • In switch-mode power circuits (SMPS), the switches are either fully on or fully off.
    • This leads to ideally zero losses in the switches when on and when off.
    • This is critical for achieving high-efficiency energy conversion.

Why do we want highly-efficient power converters?

  1. Reduce the cost of energy usage
    • Ex. For the same load (i.e. 1 kW) you will need to pay your utility more if the converter is more lossy (i.e. may need to pay for 1.2 kW)
  2. Enables more power to be delivered over existing electrical infrastructure
    • Ex. Continuous current is typically limited to 80% of breaker rating. For a 15 A breaker at home, you can supply 0.8 × 15 A × 120 V = 1.44 kW to the load at 100% efficiency - but only 0.72 kW if the converter is 50% efficient.
  3. Reduce the size of the power converter (volume, weight)
    • Heat needs to be extracted.
